cards.front: Recall a key point about Criminal Defences
cards.back: Defences allow a defendant to avoid criminal liability even if the prosecution has proved actus reus and mens rea

cards.front: Recall a key point about Criminal Defences
cards.back: Self-defence is available where the defendant used reasonable force to defend themselves, another person or property

cards.front: Recall a key point about Criminal Defences
cards.back: The force used must be proportionate to the threat — excessive force negates the defence of self-defence

cards.front: Recall a key point about Criminal Defences
cards.back: Insanity is governed by the M'Naghten rules — the defendant must have a defect of reason from a disease of the mind

cards.front: Recall a key point about Criminal Defences
cards.back: Under M'Naghten, the defendant must not know the nature and quality of their act or that it was wrong

cards.front: Recall a key point about Criminal Defences
cards.back: Automatism is an act done by the body without the mind's control — it negates actus reus (e.g. sleepwalking, convulsion)

cards.front: Recall a key point about Criminal Defences
cards.back: Involuntary intoxication can be a defence if it prevents the defendant forming mens rea — but not for crimes of basic intent

cards.front: Recall a key point about Criminal Defences
cards.back: Voluntary intoxication is only a defence to specific intent crimes (e.g. murder, s18 GBH) — not to basic intent crimes

cards.front: Recall a key point about Criminal Defences
cards.back: Duress applies where the defendant was compelled to commit a crime by threats of death or serious injury

cards.front: Recall a key point about Criminal Defences
cards.back: Duress is not available for murder or attempted murder, and the threat must be immediate and inescapable

cards.front: Recall a key point about Criminal Defences
cards.back: Necessity is a rare defence where the defendant breaks the law to avoid a greater evil — it is very strictly limited

cards.front: Recall a key point about Criminal Defences
cards.back: Consent can be a defence to some offences — but not to serious harm except in recognised exceptions (sport, surgery)

cards.front: What should you know about gcse law exam tips — criminal defences?
cards.back: 1. For Criminal Defences questions, identify the relevant area of law and state the legal principles clearly 2. Apply legal rules to the facts of the scenario — don't just state the law 3. When evaluating, consider both the effectiveness and fairness of legal rules 4. Reference relevant cases and statutes when discussing Criminal Defences 5. Consider reform proposals and alternative approaches where relevant
